heading: Scheduling: Yon
summary: Schedule declares how often a worker runs, next to the code that runs, instead of in .tachyonrc. The worker gets the same supervisor, deadlines and bounds that a controller already gets.
body:
A worker under server/workers is a Handler class that the runtime calls with POST on a timer. Like a Spring @Scheduled method, POST takes no parameter and returns nothing. Schedule takes fixedDelaySeconds (from 1 to 86400) and the optional initialDelaySeconds (from 0 to 86400). By default, initialDelaySeconds is one full interval. A .tachyonrc worker has always worked this way. There is no cron field. A cron expression is a calendar schedule written as text. It needs a parser and a time zone policy, and the runtime has neither. A limited worker really needs only a fixed delay. A source declares its cadence (how often it runs) in exactly one place: the annotation or .tachyonrc. Declaring both fails with TY1502. The annotation is removed before the worker compiles. So a worker that declares nothing else gets no extra runtime code at all. Tac has no equivalent. A browser page has no supervisor (a process that runs and watches other work) to run a separate timer. So this annotation exists in only one realm. In Lua the marker is a comment line, `-- @Schedule({...})`, above the Handler table.

C++ has no tab here, because C++ Yon code has only route controllers so far: the build refuses `Schedule` in C++ with `TY1502` (ADR 0099).
